analysis.one_liner: Restores federal pre-approval of voting rule changes in states with recent discrimination records and adds polling protections on tribal lands.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 179 Democratic cosponsors, but the House Judiciary Committee never acted on it, and it died when the 114th Congress ended without a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court struck down the old formula in 2013 for deciding which states needed federal approval before changing election rules, this bill would have written a new one: any state with 15 or more voting-rights violations over the previous 25 years (or 10, with at least one by the state itself) would have to clear new voting changes with the Justice Department or a federal court for 10 years [S2] [S3]. It would also require states to provide polling places, early voting, and registration services on tribal lands when tribes request them [S2] [S3], require public notice whenever voting rules or polling resources change [S2] [S3], and make it easier for voters to get a court order pausing a suspicious rule change near an election [S2] [S3]. The bill was introduced in June 2015, referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in racial and language minority groups, especially Native American voters who often live far from polling places, and any voter harmed by late or unpublicized changes to voting rules. States and counties with clean records could opt out through a court finding, so the burden falls only on jurisdictions with recent violations [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: A state (and all its subdivisions) would become subject to federal preclearance for 10 years if it had 15 or more voting-rights violations in the previous 25 years, or 10 violations including at least one by the state itself; individual counties with 3 or more violations would also be covered, and jurisdictions with clean records could win exemption through a declaratory judgment [S2] [S3].

Tribes could request polling places, absentee and early voting locations, and voter registration offices on tribal lands, provided by the state at no cost to the tribe, with equal poll workers, hours, and equipment as elsewhere in the state [S2] [S3].

States and counties would have to give public notice within 48 hours of changing voting rules or polling place resources, and publish demographic and district data when they redraw boundaries, so voters can see and challenge changes before an election [S2] [S3].

Courts would be required to grant a preliminary injunction pausing a challenged voting practice if the plaintiff raises a serious question about its legality and the hardship balance favors the voter, giving due weight to the right to cast an effective ballot [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State and local election officials in jurisdictions with recent voting-rights violations, who would bear the cost of submitting voting changes for federal review, providing extra polling infrastructure on tribal lands, and publishing notice of changes [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Preclearance requires jurisdictions to seek Justice Department approval or a three-judge federal court ruling before implementing voting changes, adding administrative cost and delay for election officials even when the change is benign [S3].

The coverage formula counts violations over 25 years and consent decrees or settlements, so some officials argued it could keep jurisdictions covered for past conduct long after practices had changed, though the bill includes a declaratory judgment exit for jurisdictions with clean records [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would restore federal review of voting changes for jurisdictions with demonstrated recent records of voting discrimination, at the cost of added paperwork and federal oversight for election officials in those places, with an exemption path for clean records. The strongest objection is the administrative burden and the breadth of the violation-counting formula; the strongest case for it is that voting discrimination is hard to undo after an election has already been held. No serious effort was made to test either case against opposition, since the bill never advanced in committee [S5].

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee referred the bill to a subcommittee and never took it up, and although a member filed a discharge petition to try to force it to the floor, the petition did not succeed and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017 [S5].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 24, 2015 by Rep. Terri Sewell of Alabama and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1] [S5].
On July 9, 2015 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice, where no further action occurred [S5].
The bill attracted 179 cosponsors, all of them Democrats [S4].
On June 15, 2016, Rep. Pete Aguilar filed a discharge petition (Petition No. 114-4) seeking to force the bill out of committee and onto the floor [S5].
The bill never received a committee markup or a House floor vote, and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 with the bill unenacted [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local election officials in jurisdictions that would have faced federal preclearance or new transparency and tribal polling requirements are better off, since they face no new federal review of voting changes. The bill's backers ended the Congress with 179 cosponsors but nothing enacted.

industries.industry: State and local election officials in jurisdictions with recent voting-rights violations
industries.note: The bill would require these jurisdictions to submit new voting rules for federal or court preclearance, provide extra tribal polling infrastructure, and publish detailed notices of voting changes [S3]. Their interest in avoiding federal oversight runs against the voters the oversight is designed to protect.

The bill lets federally recognized tribes demand polling places, early voting and registration services on tribal lands at government expense, addressing the long travel distances that suppress Native voter turnout [S2] [S3].
